problem.title: Large-scale document classification
problem.context: An insurer receives between two and eight million documents a day (scanned forms, e-mails, PDFs) and classifies each one into one of 60 claim types with an LLM-based classifier. Volume varies strongly over the year: storm season brings four times the usual load. Three teams use the results: claims handling, fraud investigation and analytics. The documents contain personal data.

requirements.text: Classify every incoming document into a claim type, with a confidence.
Deliver the results to the three consuming teams.
Send the documents the classifier is unsure about to human review, and use the reviewers' corrections to improve the classifier.
During storm season, at eight million documents a day, every document is classified within two hours of arrival.
When classification quality drops for one claim type (for example, after a form changes its layout), operators see it within one day.
The classification costs less than 0.2 cents per document on average over the year.
A consuming team can change how it processes the results without the other teams or the classifier having to change.
The documents contain personal data and may not leave the EU.
The classifier uses an LLM from the insurer's approved provider, in its EU region.

points.description: The system ingests source events through messaging channels and uses asynchronous, message-driven serving with elastic compute scaling. Domain experts produce labels under controlled workflows; candidate models undergo offline evaluation, while version-controlled artifacts and a custom monitoring dashboard support governed deployment and adaptation.

The system ingests source events through message queues or publish-subscribe channels, then uses non-blocking messages and queues to decouple request handling from downstream training or serving work. Compute resources automatically scale with workload demand, supporting variable message volumes and asynchronous processing.

The system ingests source events and records through message queues, middleware, or publish-subscribe channels into ML data workflows. Serving instances remain stateless and independently process requests, while compute resources automatically scale with workload demand to support horizontal growth.

Domain experts produce and select labeled examples through controlled human-review workflows, creating the supervised datasets used for development. Candidate models are then evaluated offline against held-out data with trusted labels before one is selected for deployment; the choices are complementary.

The system uses active learning to identify uncertain or error-prone production inputs for labeling, producing targeted supervised examples. Candidate models are then assessed offline against held-out data with true values, and the evaluation results inform selection before deployment.

The system uses an internally tailored dashboard to monitor deployed model quality and operational behavior through model-specific checks and views. Before promotion or replacement, candidate models pass through an offline evaluation pipeline using held-out data and true values, with results informing deployment selection and subsequent monitoring.

The system evaluates candidate models offline on held-out data with true values before selecting one for deployment. After serving, it continuously or immediately monitors prediction quality and model behavior when labels become available, enabling detection of regressions or changing performance.

trajectory.hypothesis: The solution combines queued ingestion and delivery, demand-based scaling, expert review with offline prompt checks, and custom monitoring with artifact tracking.
trajectory.observation: The point captures the main mapped choices, and the description is coherent, but it is not attested as a complete combination. The space warns that evaluation requires workflow coordination and asynchronous serving requires a serving interface, neither of which is included. The choices support the stated functions, while the solution provides no measured evidence for the two-hour or cost targets; its weekly sample and week-over-week alert also do not establish one-day visibility of a true quality drop.

trajectory.hypothesis: R2 and Q4 call for messaging and asynchronous communication, while Q1 calls for demand-responsive capacity.
trajectory.observation: The region is supported by the accepted evidence for each value, and it groups well with the variable storm-season load and independent consumer groups. The space attests no source to the whole combination. Autoscaling is directionally useful, but no throughput measurement shows that it meets the deadline.

trajectory.hypothesis: A stateless, horizontally scaled serving alternative may also support Q1, but may provide less direct support for R2 and Q4 than message-driven delivery.
trajectory.observation: This contrast remains plausible for scaling, so autosynchronous messaging is not proven uniquely necessary for Q1. Stateless replicas do not by themselves deliver results independently to three consumer groups; the solution's queue choice is a free architectural choice that directly serves decoupling, although another delivery mechanism could also do so.

trajectory.hypothesis: R3 calls for expert corrections to become labels, and the correction set gives the team material to evaluate before changing the prompt.
trajectory.observation: The human-labeling and offline-evaluation combination is attested by two sources and matches the review-and-check loop. The solution's monthly replacement of examples is a prompt update, not model retraining; that update mechanism has no direct value in this space. The reviewers' labels and pre-switch check make the R3 improvement loop credible.

trajectory.hypothesis: Could active-learning sample selection substitute for the human review choice while preserving R3?
trajectory.observation: Active learning is also supported and can select uncertain examples, but it does not itself provide the claims staff corrections explicitly required by R3. The solution's human review choice is forced for the correction part of R3; selecting the uncertain items automatically could be combined with it, but that combination is not the solution described.

trajectory.hypothesis: Q2 calls for model-specific production visibility, while Q3 and R3 make prompt changes and their checks relevant to continued quality and cost control.
trajectory.observation: The monitoring and evaluation combination is attested by a source, but the dashboard watches review share and mean confidence rather than verified classification quality. A weekly random review sample and a week-over-week alert cannot establish detection within one day. Batching and prompt checks may help control cost, but the solution reports no cost result.

trajectory.hypothesis: Real-time prediction-quality monitoring may better meet Q2 than a dashboard based on confidence and review share.
trajectory.observation: This contrast is attested with offline evaluation and fits the one-day visibility target more directly, conditional on labels being available. It shows that the solution's custom dashboard is not forced by Q2; the chosen dashboard is a free implementation choice and only partly meets the stated observability scenario.

regions.name: Queue-based elastic processing
regions.reason: Independent messaging consumers support delivery and loose coupling, while elastic workers respond to variable demand. The region is supported value by value, though throughput remains unmeasured and no source attests the complete combination.

regions.name: Reviewed labels and pre-change evaluation
regions.reason: Claims staff corrections supply labels and the reviewed set is used to check a prompt before promotion. The combination has direct support in the space and is required for the correction loop described by R3.

alternatives.name: Document classification as built
alternatives.summary: A Kafka-based document pipeline with a horizontally scaled LLM classifier, independent downstream consumers, human review, periodic prompt example updates, and per-claim-type monitoring.

choices.reason: Kafka messages carry uploads into the workflow; this supports scalable intake, but the requirements do not mandate this particular ingestion mechanism. Evidence accepts messaging-based ingestion (s02_p06, s15_p03).
choices.solution_quote: each upload puts a message on a Kafka topic

choices.reason: Separate consumer groups let teams read at their own pace and isolate changes. Messaging is a suitable way to achieve loose coupling, but the requirement does not force Kafka or this exact pattern. Evidence accepts asynchronous message-driven serving (s07_p01, s10_p04, s16_p04, s16_p05).
choices.solution_quote: Each consuming team has its own consumer group and reads at its own pace

choices.reason: Worker count follows backlog, which responds to seasonally variable demand and can avoid holding peak capacity all year. This is supported as an elastic-scaling choice, but no comparison or measured result establishes that it is required or meets either numeric target. Evidence accepts elastic scaling (s02_p01, s04_p02, s04_p06, s13_p09, s13_p10, s15_p04, s21_p15).
choices.solution_quote: The number of classifier workers scales with the length of the Kafka topic's backlog, from 4 to 120.

choices.reason: Human corrections are expressly required by R3, and claims staff provide them through a controlled review workflow. Evidence accepts human-in-the-loop labeling (s09_p03, s09_p04, s09_p09, s10_p08, s22_p17, s23_p09, s24_p08, s24_p09, s24_p10, s24_p11).
choices.solution_quote: Documents with a confidence below 0.7 go to a review queue in a labelling tool, where claims staff correct the claim type.

choices.reason: The reviewed set is checked before a prompt change, reducing the chance that corrections degrade classification. R3 requires using corrections to improve the classifier but does not require this specific offline evaluation method. Evidence accepts offline evaluation (s02_p09, s04_p15, s06_p08, s08_p02, s09_p04, s20_p03, s20_p09, s22_p08, s25_p09).
choices.solution_quote: checks the new prompt against 2,000 reviewed documents before switching to it

choices.reason: The custom dashboard provides a tailored per-claim-type view, but its alert is based on review share and its other metric is mean confidence; the solution does not show one-day detection of an actual quality drop. Real-time quality monitoring is a space alternative that fits Q2 more directly. Evidence accepts custom monitoring dashboards (s20_p10, s23_p03, s23_p09, s23_p11).
choices.solution_quote: A dashboard shows, per claim type, the share of documents sent to review and the mean confidence

choices.reason: Recording prompt version and model name makes results traceable to their producing artifacts. This is a useful provenance choice, but no requirement mandates artifact version control. Evidence accepts artifact version control (s12_p05, s19_p05).
choices.solution_quote: Every result is stored with the prompt version and the model name that produced it.

adrs.title: Queue-based intake, delivery, and elastic processing
adrs.context: The workflow must deliver results to three teams, let them process independently, absorb a fourfold seasonal increase, classify up to eight million documents inside two hours, and keep annual average cost below the stated limit.

options.name: Kafka messaging with backlog-scaled workers
pros: Independent consumer groups isolate teams' processing pace and changes.
Workers scale with demand instead of remaining fixed at peak capacity.
Messaging decouples arrival, classification, and delivery.
cons: No throughput benchmark establishes the two-hour objective.
No annual cost measurement establishes the cost ceiling.
options.reason: This is a well-supported fit to the variable workload and loose-coupling requirement. The broad use of queues and elastic workers is a design choice; the specific targets are not demonstrated, so Q1 and Q3 remain only partly met.

options.name: Stateless horizontally scaled serving
pros: Independent replicas can scale out with demand.
cons: Stateless replicas alone do not give each consuming team an independently paced result stream.
options.reason: This alternative remains plausible for throughput but gives less direct support to R2 and Q4 than the asynchronous message-driven solution. It is a contrast offered by the space, not an option the solution says its designers weighed.

adrs.title: Human correction and prompt evaluation
adrs.context: Uncertain documents need expert correction, and corrections must contribute to classifier improvement without introducing unreviewed regressions.

options.name: Expert labeling with offline evaluation
pros: Claims staff provide the corrected labels required by R3.
A held-out reviewed set is checked before a prompt update is promoted.
cons: The prompt examples are refreshed monthly, so improvement is not immediate.
options.reason: Human review is forced by R3's explicit requirement for reviewer corrections. Offline evaluation is a free but supported safeguard; the solution does not need this particular evaluation method to satisfy the correction requirement.

options.name: Active-learning sample selection with offline evaluation
pros: Programmatic selection can target uncertain or error-prone cases.
cons: Selection alone does not supply the human corrections required by R3.
options.reason: This space alternative could complement human labeling but cannot replace it for the stated requirement. It is a contrast offered by the space, not an option the solution says its designers weighed.

adrs.title: Production visibility and artifact traceability
adrs.context: Operators need timely visibility into class-specific degradation, and results need enough model and prompt metadata to trace their origin.

options.name: Custom per-claim-type dashboard and artifact version tracking
pros: A tailored dashboard exposes review share and confidence by claim type.
Stored prompt and model identifiers support traceability.
cons: Review share is only a proxy for classification quality.
Weekly sampling and a week-over-week alert do not show a quality drop within one day.
options.reason: The dashboard is a free implementation choice and only partly satisfies Q2. Artifact tracking is useful for traceability but is not forced by a stated requirement.

options.name: Real-time prediction-quality monitoring with offline evaluation
pros: Continuous or immediate quality measurement more directly supports the one-day detection target when labels are available.
cons: It depends on timely labels, which the solution's weekly sample does not guarantee.
options.reason: This contrast could meet Q2 more directly, conditional on label availability. It shows that the chosen custom dashboard is not forced. It is offered by the space, not an option the solution says its designers weighed.

uncovered.decision: Use an LLM as the fixed classifier and build its prompt from the 60 claim types and ten labeled examples.
uncovered.solution_quote: The prompt lists the 60 claim types with a short definition and ten labelled examples, and asks for a claim type and a confidence between 0 and 1.

uncovered.decision: Keep documents and LLM processing in the insurer's EU region to meet the residency constraint.
uncovered.solution_quote: Incoming documents land in an object storage bucket in the EU region

uncovered.decision: Preprocess scanned documents with OCR and remove duplicate content by hash.
uncovered.solution_quote: A preprocessing service reads the topic, extracts the text (with OCR for scanned forms), removes duplicates by content hash and writes the text next to the document.

uncovered.decision: Batch small documents in groups of 20 to reduce classification cost.
uncovered.solution_quote: Small documents are sent in batches of 20 to reduce cost.

uncovered.decision: Refresh prompt examples monthly using recent corrections.
uncovered.solution_quote: Every month the team replaces the prompt's examples with recent corrected documents

unaddressed.note: The solution places objects and LLM processing in an EU region, but this space has no dimension for geographic data residency or region placement.
The solution uses the approved provider's LLM in its EU region, but this space has no value for provider approval or provider-region selection.
